questions.title: Difference between Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Program-of-Thought (PoT) in DeepSeekMath?
questions.question_body: I am reading the Supervised Fine-Tuning section of the DeepSeekMath paper. The authors mention that they used a mixture of Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Program-of-Thought (PoT), and tool-integrated reasoning formats for their 776K training examples. I understand that CoT involves step-by-step natural language reasoning, but I'm not entirely clear on what constitutes a 'Program-of-Thought' approach and how it differs from 'tool-integrated reasoning'. Could someone clarify these three distinctions?

questions.title: Why did training on arXiv papers fail to improve mathematical reasoning in DeepSeekMath?
questions.question_body: In section 5.1.2, the authors state that arXiv papers seem ineffective in improving mathematical reasoning, noting that training on MathPile and ArXiv-RedPajama showed no notable improvements or even deterioration. This is surprising to me because arXiv is the primary source of high-level mathematical discourse. Is there a theoretical reason why formal scientific papers would be less useful for LLM reasoning compared to the web-scraped data in the DeepSeekMath Corpus?

questions.title: How does Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimate the baseline without a critic model?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the transition from PPO to GRPO. In standard PPO, the advantage $A_t$ is computed using a learned value function $V_{\psi}$ (the critic). The paper says GRPO "foregoes the critic model" and instead uses the average reward of multiple sampled outputs for the same question as the baseline. Looking at the objective function in Equation 3, I don't see the explicit subtraction of a baseline. How is the "relative" advantage $\hat{A}_{i,t}$ actually calculated from the group scores to achieve variance reduction without a separate network?

questions.title: Why does RL improve $\text{Maj@K}$ but not $\text{Pass@K}$ in DeepSeekMath?
questions.question_body: In the 'Why RL Works?' section (5.2.2), the authors provide a graph showing that reinforcement learning improves $\text{Maj@K}$ accuracy but does not significantly improve $\text{Pass@K}$. They conclude that RL makes the output distribution more robust by boosting the correct response from the TopK, rather than enhancing fundamental capabilities. I don't quite understand this. If the model is now more likely to sample the correct answer (increasing $\text{Maj@K}$), hasn't its fundamental ability to solve the problem actually improved?

questions.title: Understanding the 'Unified Paradigm': How does the Gradient Coefficient $GC_{\mathcal{A}}$ relate to different RL algorithms?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces a unified paradigm in Equation 8 to compare SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO, and GRPO, where the gradient is expressed as: $\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J}_{\mathcal{A}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[(q,o) \sim \mathcal{D}] \left( \frac{1}{|o|} \sum_{t=1}^{|o|} GC_{\mathcal{A}}(q, o, t, \pi_{rf}) \nabla_{\theta}\log \pi_{\theta}(o_t | q, o_{<t}) \right)$. I'm confused about how to map specific algorithms into this general formula. Specifically, what is the $GC_{\mathcal{A}}$ for Online RFT versus GRPO, and how does this coefficient explain why GRPO is more efficient at penalizing incorrect responses?
